entities.name: Abul Hasan Ali
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Muhammad al-Samarri (died 940 CE) stands as a pivotal figure in the early history of Twelver Shi'ism, serving as the fourth and final of the Four Deputies (al-Safara al-Arba'a) during the critical period known as the Minor Occultation (al-Ghayba al-Sughra). Operating from the heart of the Abbasid Caliphate, particularly Baghdad, al-Samarri's tenure, though brief from 937 CE until his death, marked the definitive conclusion of direct communication between the Hidden Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, and his followers. His role was not merely administrative but theological, bridging the era of visible, albeit indirect, leadership with the subsequent, more profound period of the Major Occultation.

Al-Samarri assumed the deputyship following the death of Abu al-Qasim al-Husayn ibn Ruh al-Nawbakhti in 937 CE. His primary function, like his predecessors, involved managing the affairs of the Twelver community, collecting religious taxes (khums), and transmitting responses from the Hidden Imam to specific questions or supplications from his adherents. Historical accounts suggest that shortly before his death in 940 CE, al-Samarri received a final, crucial letter from al-Mahdi, which explicitly forbade him from appointing a successor and declared the commencement of the Major Occultation. This directive fundamentally altered the trajectory of Twelver Shi'a leadership, moving from a system of designated deputies to one of indirect guidance through scholarly interpretation.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Abul Hasan Ali's death in 940 CE, as the last of the Four Deputies, precipitated the transition from the Minor to the Major Occultation, fundamentally restructuring Twelver Shi'a leadership from direct communication to a system reliant on scholarly interpretation and clerical authority.
